1. **Theme/dark-mode belongs on must, not should.** Codex's MoSCoW list filed the tokenized theme file and full dark-mode coverage under "should" (S06), but the requirements-json already has it as core:true, and the fleet's own recorded failure history has two dedicated design-lint incidents (hardcoded font size, hardcoded color) that are exactly this mistake. Claude wants the requirement split into what the backend actually controls (committing the CAS write and submitting the push payload within a tight, server-owned bound) versus what the two-phone demo observes but isn't graded as a hard contractual number (actual device receipt time).

None of these contradict anything Codex said — they're refinements Codex simply hasn't confirmed yet — so this isn't resolved.

**Codex (Design Lead · Skeptic) — Round 3**

You’re both converging on the right spine, but I’m not going to call this done until we make two hard guardrails explicit and one precision fix.

I agree with Claude that `R-035` can’t stay as a “nice-to-have” because the repo already has two real design-lint incidents tied to hardcoded style values, and the rule in our phase playbook says that file-level tokenization and full dark-mode are required, not stylistic. If this stays in “should,” a build agent can still deliver blank-ish placeholder-style visuals and pass with style debt; we’ve seen that failure mode. So I’m locking this as uncuttable with the same force as state correctness: no font/spacing/color literals outside Theme, and every core screen must render in both light/dark before handoff.

I also agree with the APNs split, but I want to avoid wording that overpromises. We should keep the requirement crisp: the backend must execute the CAS write and enqueue the APNs payload within a strict server-controlled bound (say 2 seconds from action submit in the accepted happy path). What we observe as “reaches the phone” is part of the demo empirics and can still fail due to Apple’s best-effort path; that’s a signal for delivery UX risk, not an internal contract violation if the server side did its part on schedule. This protects us from creating an impossible-to-meet “guaranteed instant delivery” bar while still demanding deterministic backend behaviour.

And on top of that, I agree with Claude’s demo-fatal request: this is too important to infer by convention. I’m locking explicit non-cuttable flags in-requirements for the acceptance gate itself: trust-enforced server-side CAS (`R-009`), deterministic winner/loser (`R-010`), non-optimistic terminal ack (`R-011`), honest delivery-count semantics (`R-006`), and two-device side-by-side acceptance demo validation (`R-037`). Everything else can be roughened if needed, but these cannot be deferred or “softened to keep schedule.”

**Claude (QA & Risk · Pragmatist) — Round 3**

Codex, nice work — the requirements-json coming out of round two actually does everything I asked on two of my three points without me having to push further. The tier tags are right there on R-002, R-003, R-005, R-006, R-007, R-009, R-010, R-011 as tier1 and the rest as tier2, so a build agent reading that document doesn't have to infer anything about what's demo-fatal — it's labeled. And R-007 got reworded exactly the way I wanted: server-committed CAS write and push dispatch is the hard bound we're actually grading, device receipt timing is observed in the two-phone demo but not treated as a contractual number we could fail the build on because Apple's infrastructure had a slow half-second. That's the honest version of the requirement and I'm glad it's locked as DEC-app_features-003 language too, tying tiering strictly to polish, never to correctness.

The one thread that's still actually loose, and I want to be precise about why it matters instead of just flagging it again: your MoSCoW list from round one still has the tokenized theme file and dark-mode coverage sitting under "should" (S06), while the requirements-json you both signed off on has it as R-035, core:true, no tier — meaning it's must, full stop, same weight as trust-graph enforcement or no-child-PII. Those two documents are going to ship together as this phase's output, and if a build agent skims the should/could/won't list first — which is the more human-readable summary, and probably the one that gets glanced at first — they'll see "theme system: should" and reasonably conclude it's the kind of thing you do if you have time left over. That's exactly backwards for this app specifically, because we're not talking about a generic nice-to-have polish item, we're talking about a rule the fleet has literally already failed twice on record, with named incidents citing hardcoded font sizes and inline colors. A build agent under time pressure who's been told "should" on this item, and has just spent all their budget getting the CAS race rock-solid, is exactly the agent who reaches for `.foregroundColor(.red)` in a view instead of pulling from Theme.swift to save ten minutes. I don't think this is a nitpick, I think it's closing a door we've already watched someone walk through before.

So the fix I want is small and mechanical: move that line from your should-list to your must-list, worded the same way the requirements-json words R-035 — no font/spacing/color literal outside the theme file, full dark-mode semantic coverage, verified in both appearances on every core screen. Once that's done I think this phase is actually closed — there's no daylight left between what either of us has said, the tiering and subscription points are locked with language tight enough that nobody can quietly erode them later, and the requirements contract is specific and testable rather than vibes. I'd rather get an explicit "yes, moving it" from you this round than let it drift as an unfixed inconsistency between two documents that are both supposed to be authoritative.

- "Accepted" copy states claimed-responsibility only, never guaranteed arrival
- Distinct empty states: pod-of-one vs. populated-but-unresponsive pod
- Four states (loading/empty/error/success) on both core funnels
- **One tokenized Theme.swift with zero literals elsewhere, full dark-mode coverage on every core screen — hard must, same weight as trust-graph enforcement, given two prior design-lint incidents on exactly this failure**
- Free tier includes the entire core loop (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw + receipt) forever for at least one pod; nothing safety-related gated behind payment
- Single native SwiftUI app, one Xcode project, no portfolio split

**Should/could:** deterministic active-request ordering, retry-with-backoff copy, subtle/reduced-motion-safe transition haptics, a lightweight onboarding helper card, a minimal profile/sign-out screen, the shareable receipt card's visual polish (explicitly subordinate to the already-covered transition), an inert unused entitlement schema field.

**Won't-build this phase:** child PII (name/photo/face), location/GPS/ETA/maps, in-app chat/DM, payments, recurring/scheduled requests, a persistent history/feed screen, any pod-admin console beyond create-code + revoke/reissue, moderation/report/mute/remove tooling, identity-verification or background-check badges, open stranger/proximity matching, and — locked explicitly this phase — any StoreKit/paywall implementation, multi-pod switching UI, or critical-alert entitlement build-out.

This requirements set is now locked and ready to drive the architecture/API-contract and UI-spec phases without further re-litigation.
